newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asia Grain - Japan to buy corn, eyes China origin.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Grain - Japan to buy corn, eyes China origin.

text.p: Japanese buyers said on Monday they will continue to buy U.S. corn this week for April/June shipment, but are carefully watching its price competitiveness against South American and Chinese grain.
"We're watching whether the price rises in the Chicago market will continue and by how much," a senior official at a Japanese feed maker said.
"That will be a factor in deciding to buy Chinese corn.
China is still offering corn to Japanese importers, but its export prices remains less competitive against U.S. origins, traders said. The Japanese are also taking a look at corn from South America.

The Chicago corn futures market rallied on Friday on aggressive fund buying, and the March contract touched a session high of US$2.92-1/2 per bushel, the highest level since it reached $2.95-1/4 a bushel last October 16.
Japanese trade houses have bought up to 80 percent of their April/June corn requirements so far, traders said.
U.S. corn premiums were quoted at between 97 and 100 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT May contract compared with about 97 cents last week, traders said.
Japanese importers are buying U.S. soybeans for April shipment and premiums were quoted at about 117 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT March position, almost unchanged from last week, traders said.
The firmer tone in freight rates is behind the slight rise in premiums, they said.
U.S. Gulf/Japan freight rates rose to $27 a tonne for nearby shipment, from $26.50 last week. Rates firmed on steady demand for vessels to ship steel and coal, shipping sources said.

Freight rates to South Korea from the U.S. Pacific Northwest rose to $14.50-$15.00 a tonne from $14.00 a week ago, a dealer with a Seoul-based trading house said. The rate from the U.S. Gulf also reached $24.50-$25.00 a tonne.

Taiwanese traders said freight costs from the Pacific Northwest may rise if damage to Zen-Noh Grain Corp's loading elevator in Louisiana caused delays along the Mississippi river. The elevator could be closed up to three weeks, they said.
Taiwan and the Philippines are also expected to enter the grains market this week, traders in both countries said.

Taiwan is seen tendering for 69,000 tonnes of wheat and up to 108,000 tonnes of soybeans and corn from the United States, traders said. Manila-based flour mills, on the other hand, will slip into the market on price dips, the dealers added.
Taiwanese buyers are likewise becoming interested in Argentine corn for April and May shipment following the recent rise in U.S. futures prices.

The state-owned National Food Authority (NFA) in Manila may negotiate for more supplies of rice from either Thailand or China after clinching a deal last week to buy 200,000 tonnes of rice from Vietnam.
In South Korea, corn buyers are likely to hold back their purchases this week due to higher U.S. prices, traders said.
Buyers who were expected to snap up to 112,000 tonnes of corn for April shipment now appear likely to postpone their purchases for the time being, they said.
But South Korean interest in small cargoes of Chinese corn for delivery to minor ports remains strong, traders said.
"There is still good demand for Chinese corn," a trader with Cheiljedang Corp said.
A trader with the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) said it bought three 12,500-tonne cargoes of Chinese corn last weekend for about $141.90 a tonne C&F.
The only likely purchase from South Korea this week is for about 21,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat for April shipment, traders said.
